inline.s: In the preceding section the World-Honored One had already spoken of prajñā-pāramitā as an illusion (“The Buddha speaks of prajñā-pāramitā, which is not prajñā-pāramitā, and so is called prajñā-pāramitā”). Not only that, but even the Dharma this sutra itself teaches—the Diamond prajñā-pāramitā—is likewise an illusion.

Next the World-Honored One takes the perfection of patience as an example, showing that the six perfections are also illusions: do not cling to marks, but be free of all marks, and only then can the mind be without obstruction and pass beyond all suffering and distress.
Subhuti! The perfection of patience, which the Tathāgata says is not the perfection of patience, and so is called the perfection of patience.

The World-Honored One also said: Subhuti! The perfection of patience (present as a mark), which the Tathāgata says is not the perfection of patience (empty of self-nature), and so is called the perfection of patience (illusory). This says that the perfection of patience is an illusion, and one must not cling to the mark of the perfection of patience.

[The perfection of patience] is the perfection of patience among the six perfections (giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, prajñā). The old translation of the six perfections is the six pāramitās. “Pāramitā” means arriving at the other shore; in Chinese it is rendered “crossing over” (the same as “ferrying across”), meaning to cross over to the other shore (the shore of nirvāṇa). “Patience” ordinarily means being put to shame or insulted. In fact, in classical Chinese “patience” also carries the meaning of being thwarted and harmed. Master Xuanzang translates the six perfections as: giving, pure precepts, patient endurance, vigor, still reflection, and prajñā. This shows that patience here means peaceful endurance. Therefore, the perfection of patience is: when persons, affairs, and circumstances go against one's intent (vexing and harming), one does not give rise to anger and malice. The heart of patience can guard against the invasion of outer conditions, and is therefore likened to a robe. When the practitioner puts on the robe of patience, he is like a warrior wearing armor, protected from harm.

Therefore, the key to dealing with vexation is not to be turned by conditions but to turn them—to know that vexation is originally an illusion, to give rise to neither anger, hatred, nor rejection, and so the mind is without obstruction, passing beyond all suffering and distress, turning affliction into bodhi, gaining only the benefit and receiving no harm. Remember: Māra is born of the mind, and by the mind is also extinguished. When insulted:

Think of it as expunging karmic retribution. This retribution is self-made and self-received; one should not resent or blame others. Moreover, once it is settled it is settled, and the debt of wrong is wiped clean in a single stroke—a very good thing.

Think of it as a blessing arriving in reverse. Realize that this is a blessing coming against you, and it comes to bring your spiritual practice to completion. Mencius said: “When Heaven is about to lay a great responsibility upon a person, it will first embitter his mind and will, tax his sinews and bones, starve his body, empty his resources, and disorder his undertakings, so as to stir his mind, steady his nature, and augment what he is unable to do.” For the one cultivating the Way, everyone is bringing me to completion; all are my benefactors. Some aid me through favorable conditions, others through conditions adverse yet favorable; all are causing my spiritual work to ripen. I have not even time enough to be grateful—how could I resent? I have only benefactors, no enemies.

Look upon it as an examination question on the path of bodhi. It tests whether one's practice has real power, and through this tempering the practice advances a further storey, so liberation becomes all the more certain. The practitioner faces such an examination at all times and in all places: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” “Do not grasp at marks; abide in the unmoving thusness.”—In the midst of the illusion, did you take it for real? Did your mind stir? How the practice fares can itself be tested thus.

The practice of patience has three levels: first, endure first and then dissolve; second, endure and dissolve at once; third, not even to be aware of it. Here I will give an instance of the practice of patience: “Met with cold glares, yet as if bathed in a spring breeze.”
The Elder Master Guangqin, at

years of age, entered the rear mountain to practice austerities, without food or clothing, passing through thirteen winters and summers. Shortly after he returned to Chengtian Monastery, the incense-offering money set out in the great hall went missing. When the master of the monastery and the keeper of the hall lamp spread the news, the whole monastery was in an uproar. Before he came back, the incense money had never been lost; not long after his return, the incense money the whole monastery relied on for its livelihood vanished without a trace—and what made everyone think at once was that he sat in meditation in the great hall every night. If anyone had laid hands on it, the first to know should have been he; since he showed no reaction, who was the most likely suspect for stealing the incense money? In everyone's mind the answer went without saying. From then on, up and down the monastery, although none spoke it aloud, whenever they met Master Guangqin they greeted him with nothing but cold, hostile looks. The ancients said: “When ten thousand fingers point at a man, he dies though he is not ill.” Under the silent censure of the whole assembly, he let out not a single word of self-justification, and stirred not the least thought of discontent or resentment. So he passed more than a week, with all still glaring at him in anger, yet he remained as if bathed in a spring breeze. Only then did the master of the monastery and the keeper of the hall lamp come forward and unfold the riddle of this case. It turned out the incense money had never been lost—the two masters had only meant by this to test Master Guangqin, to see what sort of skill the thirteen years on the mountain had forged! They had not expected that he should be as if bathed in a spring breeze amid the assembly's anger. With this explanation by the master and the lamp keeper, the whole community was filled with shame—that for this week and more the object of their daily angry glare had been a man of perfect character, a cultivator wholly transcendent of the world. Besides the pang of shame and unease, they felt all the more a pang of admiration and praise. Yet Master Guangqin remained exactly as he had been, unmoved by praise or blame, by gain or loss. (See The Cloud-and-Water Record of the Elder Monk Guangqin.)
Why so? Subhuti! When in the past I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

The World-Honored One further clarifies: Why must one realize that the perfection of patience is an illusion? Because when in the past I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, at that time I knew all this to be illusion (no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life), and so I endured peacefully without anger.

The World-Honored One is saying: When in former days I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, had I taken the perfection of patience—which is originally an illusion—to be real, then I would have had a mark of a self, a mark of a human, a mark of a being, a mark of a life, and, unable to bear the other's unreasonableness and cruelty, would have given rise to anger and hatred and failed to reach the perfection of patience.

Patience has two kinds: first, the forced endurance that takes the insult to be real; second, the realization that the insult is an illusion—awake eyes watching a dream, and so there is naturally nothing to mind. The latter is the most excellent and lofty. With no self and no human, from where does the insult come? Since the insult does not exist, what need is there to endure? This endurance that does not endure is the great patience. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp

Chapter Twenty-seven records: “Master Sengzhao (one of the four outstanding disciples of Master Kumārajīva), encountering the calamity of the ruler of Qin, on the point of execution recited this verse: The four great elements have no master of their own; the five aggregates are from the outset empty. Setting my head before the bright blade is like cutting the spring breeze (as though the spring wind passed through; “cutting the spring breeze” is an inversion, i.e., the spring breeze cuts).” The Tower Inscription of Master Hanshan at the Five-Peak of Mount Lu records: Master Hanshan, “when tortured in the imperial prison, suddenly entered meditation. The blows of the cane, the needle, and the burn were as if striking wood and stone.” The Collected Works of the Old Man Zibai records: Master Zibai, “when interrogated, though old and frail, passed through every kind of pain and torture, so that all his attendants felt their hearts sink, yet the Master was as a cloud at ease and water at rest, with not a single thing amiss.”

[King Kali] In former days, when the Buddha was practicing on the causal ground, there was a King Kali, of violent, evil, and arrogant nature. At that time the Buddha was practicing meditation outside the city. King Kali led his palace women out to wander and view the sights. The court ladies abandoned the king and came to the Buddha's place, and the Buddha expounded the Dharma for them. When the king saw this he gave rise to an evil mind and asked the Buddha: “Have you attained the fruit of the arhat?” The Buddha said: I have not. “Have you attained the fruit of the anāgāmin?” The Buddha answered: No. The king said: “Then do you, with a body still full of greed and the afflictions, recklessly gaze at women?” The Buddha said: Though I have not yet cut off the bond of greed, within my heart there is truly no attachment. The king then tested him: he cut off the Buddha's ears, yet his countenance changed not at all. The ministers remonstrated with the king, hoping to make him stop, but the king would not listen. He went further to cut off the nose (read “yì”) and the hands, yet the marks of his excellent form remained full and complete without the least change. Then a great rain of sand and stones fell from the sky. The king's heart was filled with terror, and he came to the Buddha, repentant and ashamed, begging for pity. The Buddha said: My heart has neither anger nor greed. The king said: “Great Virtue, how do you know that your heart has no anger and hatred?” The Buddha said: If I had no anger, then let this body be restored as it was. Having made this vow, his body was at once restored. The king was all the more repentant and ashamed, and so entered the gate of the Buddha. [The bond of greed] is one of the five bonds. The affliction of greed and desire binds beings to the births and deaths of the three realms, so that they cannot attain release. The five bonds are: the bond of greed, the bond of anger, the bond of pride, the bond of envy, and the bond of miserliness. “Bond” is another name for the afflictions, because the afflictions can bind and fetter beings, causing them to transmigrate in the three realms.

The World-Honored One uses his own experience to show that only by not clinging to marks can one truly endure; only by not clinging to marks can one fail to give rise to habitual reactions amid conditions. This also confirms that the absence of the four marks is the wondrous method for subduing the mind (see the third section).
The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra
Volume Twenty-two

Chapter Sixty-eight, on the Six Perfections Absorbing One Another, says: “The Buddha said: When a bodhisattva abides in the perfection of vigor, from the first stirring of the mind of enlightenment even to the sitting at the bodhimandala, if in the midst of these a man or a non-man comes to dismember him joint by joint, the bodhisattva thinks: ‘Who is cutting me? Who is severing me? Who is robbing me?’ And again he thinks: ‘I have gained a great, good benefit. For the sake of beings I take on a body, and beings themselves come to take it.’ At that time the bodhisattva rightly recollects the true character of all dharmas, and holding this merit, shares it with beings and directs it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, not toward the ground of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is the bodhisattva abiding in the perfection of vigor, gaining the perfection of patience.”
[Vīrya] is translated in Chinese as “vigor,” one of the six perfections. [Kṣānti] is translated as “patience,” one of the six perfections.

Master Hanshan said: “All beings' implements of birth and death, of suffering, are all brought into being by the existence of a self; the utmost bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, are all reached by the absence of a self. Because the self opposes things, right and wrong arise; when right and wrong arise, love and hate are established; when love and hate are established, joy and anger multiply; the self-nature is befouled and the ground of the mind grows clouded; when the mind is clouded, all evils grow; when all evils grow, all suffering gathers; when all suffering gathers, birth and death lengthen! All of these come of the self—how grave it is! The harm of the self, like a strong city with mighty soldiers, is it easy to break? . . . Therefore, at the moment of a single rising thought test it with patience; at a single step and move, let patience lead; at turning and moving and adjusting the appearance, hold to patience; at joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, examine by patience. Thus the mind dares not stir at random, the body dares not act at random, affairs dare not be done at random, the feelings dare not break forth at random. Hence the old master (Laozi) said: Dare not be first in the world. To dare not—that is another name for patience. Because one dares not be first in the world, patience is the first practice in becoming a Buddha. Thus patience is great and the self is small, so the robe of patience can cover me and can also cover things; the virtue of benefiting oneself and benefiting others goes no further than this. Therefore it is said: The soft and harmonious robe of patience—this is the reason.” (From the Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to the Meditator Fajin.)

Whether one has a reliable hold on transcending birth and death can be tested from two ends: first, the end of favorable circumstances and success; second, the end of adverse circumstances and affliction—whether in both one has detached from marks: not giving rise to a stirring thought before conditions, not chasing after conditions.
Why so? When in the past I was dismembered limb by limb, if I had had a mark of a self, a mark of a human, a mark of a being, a mark of a life, I should have given rise to anger and hatred.

Why must one be without the four marks? On that day, when I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, had I taken this dismembering limb by limb as real (having a mark of self, human, being, life), I would have given rise to anger and hatred.

To know illusion is at once to be free of it; to be free of illusion is at once to be awake. Since there is no self, where is the insult? Without a self, who is there to suffer the insult? This is the method of drawing away the firewood from beneath the cauldron.

The World-Honored One, when formerly dismembered limb by limb, was without the four marks because he had realized in person “all marks whatsoever are false and vain” and “knowing that all dharmas have no self, he attained the patience [of non-arising].” How does one realize this in person? Master Hanshan, in the Dream Wandering Collection

Addressed to the Attendant Qi in the Boat on the Way to Leiyang, gives a most penetrating discourse—in the midst of the dharmas of arising and ceasing, to pass through conditions and test the mind, intimately breaking it through, until one reaches the ground of no doubt and then stops. I transcribe it here:
The Buddhas and patriarchs teach people, amid birth and death, to realize at once the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas
(“The patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas,” for short the non-arising patience, means true wisdom abiding in the true character of the real, which neither arises nor ceases)

, and they always marvel that people, amid the non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing. This speech is like telling the affairs of a dream to the people in the marketplace; those who hear it are not without being moved to open their eyes
(listeners are never untouched and stirred)

, but they have not yet realized the truth. In sum, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients so valued realization in person because they simply wanted, amid the dharmas of birth and death, to break through intimately—there is nothing else extraordinary about it. I have seen children afraid of ghosts: whenever they walk at night, a thing seems to follow them and they are seized with terror; though the loving mother tells them kindly that there is nothing, they still will not believe, and only after they come to believe themselves without doubt do they stop. Once one reaches the ground of no doubt, even if one frightens him with a false ghost, he will but laugh and let it go.

I once traveled on the frontier, riding by night with some strong fellows. By the side of the road was a rock; all at once the horse caught sight of it and was fiercely startled, almost throwing me to the ground. Then I
(thereupon)
reined in the horse, spurred it on with all my strength, and led it round the rock several dozen times, still drawing it on to look closely
(still leading the horse to look carefully, to be clear that this was a rock and not a monster)

. After a long while, only then did I release it to run on; from that time on, the horse encountered nothing that startled it. Because of this I know that a man traveling the perilous roads of birth and death, passing through conditions and testing the mind, must do it exactly like this and only then be done
(spur the horse around the rock and make it look closely, until it is without doubt and without fear, and only then is it done)
. Therefore the Avataṃsaka uses Sudhana to represent realization
(therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra uses the boy Sudhana's fifty-three pilgrimages to show clearly how to realize in person)
, and the hundred cities he passed through and the many teachers he sought. Even when it came to the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, he also hesitated
(hesitating, wavering)
and waited for encouragement before entering. And once he entered, he indeed gained the cool and great gate of liberation
(realizing in person that the mountain of knives and mass of fire are illusions)
. Is this not what is meant by spurring the horse around the rock and making it look closely?
(Is it not exactly making him “spur the horse around the rock and look closely,” so that he intimately breaks through?)
Viewed in this way, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other excellence—they are only able to look closely upon the marks of the world
(variant: jian)
(the world)

. Is it not birth and death and misfortune that can be frightened by men? The Buddhas and patriarchs want people to realize the non-arising patience in the midst of them, and moreover plainly say that in the midst of the non-arising they falsely see arising and ceasing
(the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the non-arising; sentient beings, within the still non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing)
. Alas! What can this really mean?
(if it were not)
If it were not that, having looked closely, one arrives of oneself at the ground of no doubt, I think that even the gracious Lord's kind admonition would hardly
(perhaps) escape being startled and frightened as well.
I
(I, in these days)
because of spreading the Dharma suffered calamity, offending the holy wrath
(the Master, for spreading the Dharma, was slandered; the emperor's wrath was stirred; he was arrested and thrown into prison, tortured under severe interrogation, his life and death uncertain)
, like a peal of thunder in broad daylight, so that those who heard it stopped up their ears. From my arrest until my release
(banished and sent away from the capital)

, more than two hundred days, I endured every kind of bitter affair beyond words. From beginning to end, as I looked within myself, that one thought of joy in no way diminished from my usual days; those who saw it were all astonished and called it extraordinary. Yet birth and death and misfortune—others were indeed alarmed for me; and when they saw that my joyful thought did not diminish, they were alarmed again. I am not alarmed at what alarms them, and they are alarmed at what does not alarm me—in this there may be a Way!

Attendant Qi, undeterred by a journey of three thousand li, came to the difficulty and questioned me in the dark prison. Soon, by the holy grace, I was exiled to the land of Lingnan, and Qi accompanied me on the boat; I write this to bid farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is precisely what men fear, and is this not—to hear that my joy did not diminish—like listening to the affairs of a dream?

(At the moment of life and death—this is precisely what men are frightened by; and to hear that my joyful thought did not diminish in the least, is it not just like listening to a man speak of the affairs of a dream?)
Hereafter I shall test you in the field of still extinction; do not take today's words as dream-speech

(in days to come, when you realize the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (in the field of still extinction), you will of yourself verify that what I say is true. [The field of still extinction] is the realm of the realization of the non-arising patience—when delusion is exhausted and the true is revealed, still extinction is present)
, do not take today's words as dream-speech
(From the Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang.)

Subhuti! Again I recall that in the past, over five hundred lives, I practiced as the ascetic of patience. In those lives, I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

The World-Honored One continued: Subhuti! Again I recall that in the past I practiced as the ascetic of patience for five hundred lives. In those five hundred lives, I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

[The ascetic of patience] Shakyamuni Buddha, on the causal ground, was the ascetic of patience, cultivating the practice of patience. [In those lives] In those five hundred lives. “Those” means that; “lives” refers to the “five hundred lives” of the preceding sentence. The Tang
Yijing translation reads: “Again I recall that in the past, over five hundred lives, I was an ascetic of patience. At that time I had no such thoughts as these.”

Master Yongjia's Song of Certifying the Way says: “My teacher (Shakyamuni Buddha) was allowed to see Dīpaṃkara Buddha because for many kalpas he had been an ascetic of patience.” This says that the World-Honored One, when practicing on the causal ground, was able to see Dīpaṃkara Buddha and receive the prophecy because for many kalpas he had been an ascetic of patience. From this we see that the single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice in becoming a Buddha.

Those who study the Diamond Sutra all share one question: how can one be free of the four marks? Where does one begin? The starting point of freeing oneself from the four marks is to cultivate the perfection of patience: whatever is done, one should bear it. At all times and everywhere, bear it, test it, and keep on. At first the self is great and the patience small; then the patience is great and the self small; by vigorous, unflagging effort, persevering, one reaches the absence of the mark of a self. Once the mark of self is extinguished, the other three marks are gone with it. The four marks are illusion, and the perfection of patience is also illusion; yet to use illusion to extinguish illusion, one is only the farther from illusion.

In Master Daozheng's book The Elder Master Guangqin's Practice Examinations, it is written: “On the road of practice there are examinations every day, examinations at all times. In the selection-ground of the Buddha, each person hands in his own report card.” “We may well read the Diamond Sutra early in the morning—‘all marks whatsoever are false and vain,’ ‘do not grasp at marks, abide in the unmoving thusness’—and the scripture is read this way. But suppose someone curses us very fiercely, and the things he curses us with are all unfounded; then we set the Diamond Sutra aside for the moment, take the situation as real, and begin to grieve and to feel wronged. We do not remember in the least: ‘all marks whatsoever are false and vain.’ We begin to run round and round chasing the false marks—not merely grasping at marks, but moreover stirring the mind, and not merely stirring the mind but grieving greatly, without the slightest bit of ‘abiding in the unmoving thusness.’ So having read the scriptures for decades, the moment an applied problem is set, we die on the spot. If others say that our study of Buddhism is all a deception, that we never truly practiced, we hear it and are quite unconvinced. But at the first examination we betray ourselves and show that what the Buddha taught us we have in truth not learned at all. Whatever perfection of patience—set it aside for now, argue a little first, have a good cry first.”
Therefore, Subhuti! The bodhisattva should be free of all marks and raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Subhuti! The bodhisattva should be free of all marks and raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

What was said above—that the first perfection is illusion and the perfection of patience is illusion—means one should cultivate while detached from marks. Now it goes a step further: even at the moment of raising the mind, one should raise it while detached from marks. From this we know that “free of all marks” runs through the whole bodhi path from beginning to end.

[Therefore] A word that carries the previous passage and opens the next. [Free of all marks] Free of the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, the mark of a life, as well as the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. [Raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] Raise the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings.

One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form; one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling.

One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind without love or hate, without grasping or rejecting. If the mind has a dwelling and attachment, this dwelling and attachment is itself an error.

[If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling] If the mind has a dwelling and attachment, this dwelling and attachment is not (that is, is not a true dwelling). Why? Because if the mind dwells, it is turned by conditions—this is delusion. “If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling” returns again to the question Subhuti asked at the very beginning of this sutra: “How should the mind be abided?” So the answer to “How should the mind be abided?” is: do not abide in marks.

The Collected Annotations on the Diamond Sutra says: “Master Huangbo said: . . . ‘Free of all marks, sentient beings and all Buddhas have no further difference; if only one can be without mind, that is the ultimate.’ ‘If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling’ means the mind of suchness is originally without dwelling. If one does not dwell in the marks of dharmas, one accords with the Way. If one dwells in dharmas, one goes against the right teaching; going against the right teaching, that dwelling is not a true dwelling.”

How does one not dwell in marks? The Sixth Patriarch, in the Platform Sutra, has a passage of extraordinary brilliance: “What is called thoughtlessness? If, on seeing all dharmas, the mind is not stained or attached (without love or hate, grasping or rejecting), that is thoughtlessness. Functioning, it reaches everywhere, yet dwells not anywhere. Only purify the original mind (weakening and weakening the mind of love and hate, grasping and rejecting), so that the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates and, amid the six dusts, are neither stained nor mixed; coming and going freely, in general use without obstruction—this is the prajñā samādhi, self-mastery and liberation, and is called the practice of thoughtlessness. . . . Good and wise friends! One who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness penetrates the ten thousand dharmas; one who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness reaches the stage of the Buddha.”

‘so that the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates and, amid the six dusts, are neither stained nor mixed; coming and going freely, in general use without obstruction’ and ‘functioning, it reaches everywhere, yet dwells not anywhere’—this is ‘give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.’

Here the World-Honored One again speaks of the work of guarding and spontaneous flowing: that is, guarding the mind so it does not run after conditions, and letting the mind flow freely so it does not run after conditions. The initial stage is guarding the mind (“one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas”); when the guarding is mature, one sets aside the guarding and does the work of spontaneous flowing, letting the mind flow freely. So the mind, following the desires, never oversteps the rule (“one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”). Take the cure of addiction as a metaphor: the first stage is the guarding stage—to realize deeply the harm of drugs and to keep strictly separated from them; when this is mature, it becomes the stage of spontaneous flowing—though the drug lies at one's side within easy reach, one still will not be tempted.

The addiction of sentient beings since the beginning-less kalpa is to “give rise to a mind toward conditions.” Therefore, in the guarding stage, one should still all the outer conditions and nurture the embryo of the sage. When the guarding is ripe, one should blend one's light with the dust, passing through conditions and testing the mind, realizing the wisdom of non-discrimination, so as to be like one who “passes through a garden of ten thousand blossoms without a single leaf clinging to his body.” A verse says: “Set loose the water-buffalo of Weishan; no one holds the rope by its nose. On the green willows and fragrant grass of the spring breeze bank, at ease it lies up and lies down—free.”

[Blend one's light with the dust] This means to merge with the worldly and not to set oneself apart, yet not to be stained by the evil and turbid. But it must be specially pointed out that the stage of “spontaneous flowing” begins only after the work of “guarding” is mature. [The wisdom of non-discrimination] Also called the mind of non-discrimination; when the bodhisattva, upon the first ground, enters the stage of seeing the Way, he leaves behind all discriminative thinking of feelings—the formless true wisdom. [The stage of seeing the Way] When the bodhisattva first attains the first ground, penetrating a little of the principle of the two non-selves, experiencing suchness, and for the first time seeing the middle Way, it is therefore called the stage of seeing the Way. [The two non-selves] The non-self of persons and the non-self of dharmas. The non-self of persons is realizing that the five aggregates are a false union with no real substance; the non-self of dharmas is realizing that all dharmas are like illusions, with no real substance.
Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when practicing giving. Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way.

Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in the six dusts when giving (here form represents the six dusts). Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way.

[The bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when giving] Using the dust of form to represent the six dusts (citing form, and likewise sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, and all dharmas), this means the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas when giving—that is, the bodhisattva should give while not dwelling in marks.

Master Xuanzang's Tang translation reads: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all bodhisattvas should practice giving without dwelling, and should not practice giving while dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.” [For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way] Example surpasses words; a bodhisattva who truly gives for the benefit of all beings should be free of marks. Moreover, not to give rise to a mind dwelling in form, not to give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, and to give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere—such a Dharma-giving brings beings the greatest and most fundamental benefit. Therefore, in the final section the World-Honored One says: “Subhuti! If a person gives away the seven treasures filling an immeasurable, countless number of worlds; and if a good man or good woman who has raised the bodhi mind holds to this sutra, even a four-line verse, and receives, holds, reads, recites, and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses that. How does one expound it for others? (How does one expound it for others?) Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.” The Buddha's Forty-Two Chapter Scripture says: “To feed a thousand billion Buddhas of the three times is not so good as feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without practice, and without realization.” (“Without thought and without dwelling” is the Sixth Patriarch's teaching in the preceding note; “without practice and without realization” means not producing the thought ‘I am practicing, I have realized.’ This is the one who does not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, and raises a mind that dwells nowhere.)
The Tathāgata says that all marks are not marks. Again he says that all beings are not beings.
The Tathāgata says that all marks (present as marks) are not marks (empty of self-nature). Again he says that all beings (present as marks) are not beings (empty of self-nature).

[All marks are not marks] All marks are illusions. [All beings are not beings] All beings are illusions. This sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “In the real character, there are truly no bodhisattvas and no beings. Why? Boddhisattvas and beings are all illusory transformations.”

Closely following the words above—“Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when giving. Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way”—the World-Honored One further clarifies that the marks in which one dwells and the beings one benefits are all illusions, saying: “

The Tathāgata says that all marks are not marks. Again he says that all beings are not beings.” This says: all marks and all beings are illusions. This reveals the greatest mystery: the whole universe is an illusion, a great dream! Truly hard to believe. So in what follows the World-Honored One says with great gravity: “Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference.” In order to teach us beings, the World-Honored One truly poured out his heart and blood!

Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference. Subhuti! The Dharma the Tathāgata has attained—this Dharma is neither real nor empty.

Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference. Subhuti! The Dharma of the Way that the Tathāgata has attained is neither really existing nor annihilated, but is an illusion.

[Speaker of truth] “True” means not false. [Speaker of reality] “Real” means not empty. [Speaker of suchness] Words that accord with the true character of things. [Speaker of non-deception] Not words of deceit. [Speaker of non-difference] A thousand words and ten thousand words, always one and the same, and in complete accord with all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three times. [This Dharma is neither real nor empty] The Dharma the Tathāgata has attained is neither really existing nor annihilated, but is an illusion. “Dharma” here refers to the Dharma of the Way, that is, the theory, the realm, and the fruit-ground of cultivating the Way. In the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Chapter Three, on Familiar Practice, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha and no Buddha Way.” In the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, the Buddha says: “Good men! These bodhisattvas and the beings of the last age who, practicing this mind, attain success: in this there is no practice and also no attainment (making clear that practice and attainment are both illusion). The perfect enlightenment universally illumines, still and extinction are non-dual; amid it, the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, ayutas, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are like flowers in the sky, rising and fading in confusion. Not identical, not separate; without bondage, without release. Then one knows that beings have from the outset been Buddha, and birth and death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.”

Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing. If the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors.

‘the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving’—this is a conditioned dharma; ‘the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving’—this is the unconditioned dharma.” Compare this with the passage in the fourth section, “the sublime practice of non-dwelling”: “The bodhisattva, with respect to dharmas, should dwell nowhere and practice giving”—and the understanding is the deeper.
Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing”

—the Buddha tells Subhuti: Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas, thinking that there are merit, virtue, and fruit-ground to be obtained, and so practices giving, then it is like a man in the darkness who cannot see the direction or the road.
